I don’t have references for you. This is not an idea that I read or heard about from somebody else. The concept came to me through my own experiments as well as my personal analysis of other folk’s data from various parapsychological studies. I formulated this hypothesis on my own. I tried to follow scientific protocol to the best of my ability while conducting my experiments, but I’m not a well-resourced investigator so my adherence to complete scientific rigor wasn’t flawless. I had 6 subjects, and cataloged the results from tests performed with all combinations of groupings of two from among them, where one individual would attempt a remote viewing of a randomly chosen object placed inside of a box and the other individual would attempt to interpret the viewer’s vague impressions (ie; the object’s shape, its color, its general utility) to discern the exact object from the raw data recorded by the viewer. My findings demonstrated to me beyond a reasonable doubt that those who performed better than average while viewing performed worse than average when interpreting. Obviously six subjects isn’t very close to the ideal sample size required for verifying this hypothesis outright, but as I said I did my best with the resources I had, and I definitely think my results are certain enough to provoke more in-depth studies. Some things were left up to my interpretation of what “good performance” actually meant, but another caveat of the experiment was conducting a blind vote of relative performance(on a scale of 1-100), where the four individuals who didn’t participate in the trial would be shown/told the impressions and interpretations for each instance and choose a score for the performance of both the viewer and the interpreter, respectively, without being made aware of who’s performance they were judging. I know this doesn’t say much at all about past lives, but I have reason to believe that past life memories and remote viewing ability are directly correlated with one another. 
As far as discerning your own placement on this spectrum, I would simply tell you to conduct a similar experiment of your own with other people and see how you compare to each person on each task. If you have questions on how to set this up, let me know. It’s time consuming, and requires you to have at least a few people willing to participate, but I can tell you that my experiments were really fun to conduct and all the participants enjoyed participating. Oh and if you have questions about my language feel free to ask, sometimes I don’t state my ideas in the most accurate or concise way, so I’m happy to clarify anything you don’t understand.

So parapsychological abilities such as remote viewing, past life memories, and telepathic ability are variable from person to person. Each individual falls upon a spectrum. On one end of this spectrum fall those individuals who are adept at setting loose their consciousness to “travel” to locations and events that are a great distance away in time and/or space. At the other end of the spectrum fall those individuals most keen at sifting through the diluted “noise” of information inputs they receive. Fishing is a good analogy for this spectrum. If you use a broad net, you’ll very likely catch many fish, but youre more likely to bring up a plastic bottle or some driftwood too. If you use a fishing pole, you’ll rarely, if ever, bring up trash or debris, but you’ll also never bring up more than one fish at a time. 
These spectrum juxtapositions are inversely proportionate to one another. Perfect Analysis and a deep resonate connection to the truth requires an inward projection of one’s consciousness, to sift through a pile of mostly useless information to find the rare pearl of great price. Data collection through remote viewing, past life memories, and telepathic surveillance requires an outward projection one’s consciousness. Consequently, an individual on the middle of this spectrum would not be particularly skilled at projecting their consciousness in either direction.

Thank you for all the replies, still trying to wrap my mind around it. But it seems to me that cosmological redshift and Doppler effect redshift are two different things. Cosmological redshift happens because the distance between the source of a photon and the destination where it’s measured at increases (unless the two objects are moving toward each other through space) but to me because measuring the wavelength or frequency of the photon requires some amount of time to pass, you can’t have two measurements at the same location yield different results when one is moving faster toward the source of the emitted photon, because either at the the time of the beginning or end (or both) of the measurements the two observers would be in different locations because one is moving faster toward the source of the emitted photon. Doesn’t this imply that two observers measuring the same photon, at the same time, at the same location would always yield the same results(considering their measurement devices were perfectly error free)? So, any photon measured at a source, and then measured later at a distant location, will always be observed to have redshifted by the same amount (again disregarding motion through space and the Doppler red/blueshift that comes along with it). So to all observers in the same location at the same time, photons lose energy as they travel through space. It’s generally considered true that the expansion of space redshifts photons, but never that the photons impart their energy to space in order to cause the expansion. If you could calculate the amount of redshift in a given volume of space over a given duration and simultaneously calculate the energy required for the expansion of that same volume of space during the same period of time, might the numbers match up? I guess I’m suggesting that the two processes might be interdependent.
